children: Elon Musk said he would gift every child in America one SpaceX share, following pledges by rival Anthropic and other high-profile billionaires to donate some of the immense wealth accumulating during the artificial-intelligence boom.
"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America," Musk said in a post on X early Monday. "This will be the first of many."

Shares in the company closed Friday at $146.03, and according to the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau, there are approximately 73 million children under the age of 18 living in the U.S. That could equate to Musk's giving away roughly $10 billion in stock.
SpaceX shares rose more than 1% in afternoon trading on Monday.

Musk appeared to be planning to use the government's new Trump Accounts to donate shares, according to his posts on X. The Treasury Department autoenrolled tens of millions of children in the investment accounts.

New rules set out by the Treasury last month created a path for wealthy donors to contribute stock to kids' accounts, reaching broad groups defined by age or geography. These donations, like other stock gifts, can have tax benefits for donors because they avoid capital-gains taxes and create deductions against other income.
Other details of Musk's plan weren't immediately clear. SpaceX didn't respond to requests for comment.

Musk is the world's richest person, with a net worth of more than $900 billion, a majority of which comes from his stake in SpaceX, according to a Wall Street Journal analysis earlier this year. That same analysis showed Musk has made $3.6 million an hour over his 31-year career as a tech and engineering entrepreneur.

The pledge comes a day after AI competitor Anthropic said it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new "public benefit fund" with the flexibility to make charitable donations or direct money to "specific populations."
In response, Musk suggested Anthropic should give the shares directly to the public.

The Treasury Department said that potential donors to Trump Accounts were more interested in giving if kids were going to be invested in a particular company. That differs from the broad index funds that parents' own contributions are invested in. Under the rules, families can't refuse a stock donation and generally can't sell the stock for five years.

Earlier this year, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged to donate one share to each of roughly two million American children in the Trump Accounts initiative. Michael and Susan Dell have also pledged $6.25 billion to the program.
Musk has made significant donations before. In 2021, he gave roughly $5.7 billion of Tesla shares to charity.
In the same year, Musk publicly challenged the executive director of the United Nations' World Food Program over his request for charitable donations from the ultrawealthy.

David Beasley had called on billionaires to "step up now, on a one-time basis" to tackle global hunger. "$6 billion to help 42 million people that are literally going to die if we don't reach them. It's not complicated," Beasley said during an October 2021 interview with CNN. Musk responded on social media, pledging to sell Tesla stock to fund the effort if the agency could demonstrate how $6 billion would resolve the crisis. It was unclear whether the WFP has received any funds from Musk.
